column2: One should light a lamp with ghee or with oil mixed in, and keep vigil at night; he becomes a god, no doubt.
The best of men who hear the Vaishnava story with devotion are freed from the killing of a brahmin and other sins, no doubt.
Those who circumambulate Jalashayi, the guru of the world, have circumambulated Jambudvipa, lord of men.
Then at clear dawn, having carefully satisfied the ancestors, one should perform shraddha there with worthy brahmins, best of the Pandavas —
devoted to their own wives, tranquil, avoiding others' wives, given to Vedic study, devoted to their own duties, virtuous,
always of good conduct, keeping the three twilight rites — with such as these one should have shraddha performed, if one desires one's own good.
Blessed in the human world and holy are those men who dwell at all times in the pool, the place that is Brahma's shelter,
and see Jalashayi, the leader of the gods, face to face. Whoever keeps a fortnight's fast, the auspicious chandrayana vow,
the fierce month-long fast or another supreme vow at that holy place, son of Pritha, attains heaven.
Next I shall tell the fruit of the sesame cow, and how and where it should be given, and the fruit heard of that gift.
This holy account, destroying sin, was heard in many ways by the lords of sages headed by Narada in the Naimisha forest.
This story brings long life, is holy and increases fame; whoever causes brahmins to hear it obtains all that fruit.
A cow, a house or a bed should not be given to many; a fee thus divided does not come to the giver.
She should be given to one, not to many, Yudhishthira; and if she is sold, she burns the family to the seventh generation.
Sesame is white or black, sesame is described by colour; one should make the measures of sesame for the cow and her calf.
She should be given with her calf, and not to many who desire her; whatever measure of sesame is used in a given country, after consideration,
by that measure she should be made by one who desires imperishable fruit, and worshipped carefully with sandal, flowers and unbroken rice, lord.
In the nose all perfumes are placed, in the tongue the six flavours; pearls should be set in the teeth, thighs and tail;
cotton should be placed in the belly, a lotus with gold at the navel; one should put honey and ghee on the lips and ghee on the hair;
on the dewlap one should give a blanket, on the forehead a copper vessel; pieces should be given on the shoulders and an iron rod at the joints;
one should put jaggery at the rump, honey and ghee at the hips, and as fodder milk-rice mixed with ghee and honey.
With golden horns, silver hooves and a tail adorned with pearls, with cloth and good food, and a bronze vessel for milking, she should be given.
Whatever sin was done in childhood or done unknowingly, done by speech or deed or thought in the mind,
spitting into water, stepping over a pestle, going to a vrishali, going to the guru's wife,
going to a maiden, stealing gold and drinking liquor — the sesame cow purifies all this.
She has been described by me with a day-and-night fast according to rule. The river in Yama's city known as the Vaitarani,
the place of sand where the evildoer is cooked, the pair of mountains joined to the Avichi hell,
where there are iron-beaked crows, where the place is terrifying, where the sword-leaf forest is and the burning sand —
passing over these with ease, one goes to Dharmaraja's hermitage. Seeing him, Dharmaraja speaks kind words:
A fitting canopy is spread, adorned with gems and jewels; come here, best of kings, and go to the supreme goal.
Do not give to one devoted to sin; that gift is of no great good. Not at the wrong time, not to the deformed, nor likewise to the maimed,
nor to a brahmin ignorant of the Veda or reeling with intoxication, nor to a betrayer of friends, an ingrate or one who has broken his vows.
She should be given to one versed in the Vedanta; know that. She should be given to one versed in the Vedanta, learned in the Veda, not a child,
lovely in all limbs, pure and pleasant of speech; on the full moon, the new moon and the full moon of Kartika, O Bharata,
on the full moon of Vaishakha and in Margashirsha, at eclipses of moon and sun, at the solstices, the equinoxes and at vyatipata always,
at the Shadashitimukha and at the gajachchhaya always. This rite of the sesame cow has been told to you by me, sinless one.
Piercing through the world of the sun, they go to Hari's world. All this I have told you, O king, the fruit of Chakratirtha;
by hearing or reciting it one gains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Long ago there were two fortunate danavas, Chanda and Munda; they practised austerity there on the Narmada, Yudhishthira,
meditating on the god Bhaskara, destroyer of darkness, guru of the world; pleased by them, the thousand-rayed one said:
Well done, well done, to the two, son of Pritha, on the lovely bank of the Narmada; "Chanda and Munda, name a special boon your minds desire."
Chanda and Munda said: "May we be invincible to all gods and men, lord of the gods, and free of diseases, radiant Divakara."
Bhaskara spoke to them the auspicious words "So be it"; then the Sun vanished, and by the two danavas Bhaskara
was installed with supreme devotion; whoever with senses controlled worships him gains divinity from being human, and it remains right there.
He dwells in the world of Bhaskara and in Brahma's world in the presence of the gods. One should light a lamp with ghee on every sixth day, lord of men;
he is freed from all sins and on dying goes to the city of the Sun. The holy place there is renowned as Chandraditya, best of men;
those who go to Chandraditya are always victorious.
As a garment washed by a washerman becomes spotless, so, O king, as he gazed at the unsurpassed water of the Reva,
Yama laughed, and an excellent linga rose up; then, king of kings, a bodiless voice spoke:
This holy place, Yamahasa, will always be renowned. Having bathed Shiva there, Yama went to heaven.
At Yamahasa, king of kings, one who has conquered anger and the senses, especially on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight in the month of Ashvina,
fasting with supreme devotion is freed from all sins. Keeping vigil at night one should light a lamp for the god
with ghee, king of kings; hear its fruit: one is freed from all sins arising from going to those one should not go to,
from eating what should not be eaten, from what arises from drink, from driving what should not be driven and from betraying those who should not be betrayed;
by bathing alone that manifold sin perishes; one does not see Yama's world, nor leave this, delight of Pandu.
It is a holy place on earth supremely hidden from many, prince; for those who give at Yamahasa the fruit is imperishable.
Whoever, having conquered anger, honours brahmins on the new moon, with the gift of land with devotion or the gift of sesame, O Bharata,
with the gift of a black antelope skin or the gift of a sesame cow — those who give with devotion under a good asterism and at the vriddhi yoga
cooked rice, water, a draught ox, a mighty horse, a maiden, clothing, a goat, a cow, a she-buffalo or a mare —
those who give these, best of kings, do not come near Yama; and Yama too is pleased with them in birth after birth, Yudhishthira.
Yama's mount, the female buffalo, O Bharata — by giving her there Yama is always pleased, O king;
such a one does not go to Yama's world even if burdened with sins. For this reason, son of Pritha, the gift of a she-buffalo is excellent.
A pair of woollen cloths should be made, iron-coloured, and wrapped round her; one should give her for Dharmaraja: "May he be pleased with me, best of the twice-born;
by this gift may Yama be pleased with me always." Uttering this before the brahmin — Yama's world is terrifying:
in the dreadful sword-leaf forest is the most cruel creeper of Yama, the fierce Vaitarani and the most cruel Kumbhipaka,
the most dreadful Kalasutra and likewise the twin mountains, the saw and the oil press, and at that place the most cruel vultures,
the most fierce Anishvasa and the terrible Raurava — these dreadful hells are heard of, best of the twice-born;
by his grace they become gentle, by the power of this holy place, by the power of this gift and by the power of Yamahasa;
he does not go to Yama's world and never sees hell.
With the five nectars and cow's products mixed with sesame, devoted, making offerings to the ancestors and pinda offerings according to rule,
especially on the full moon of the month of Shravana, an imperishable satisfaction is obtained until the deluge.
The supreme secret of the ancestors rests on the water of the Reva, giving release to all beings, made by the bulls among sages.
Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Vyasatirtha, hard for men to reach, son of Pritha, situated in the sky.
Yudhishthira said: "Why is Vyasatirtha situated in the sky? Tell me this briefly, without the full extent of the text."
Markandeya said: Well done, well done, mighty-armed one, righteous and devoted to your elders, devoted to your own dharma, son of Pritha, respectful of pilgrimage.
Vyasatirtha is hard for all creatures to reach, lord of men; overcome by old age and infirmity, lord of men,
I have become as if senseless, delight of Pandu; this holy place, more secret than the secret, I have told to no one.
Time itself may not dwell there, by Vasava's command, king of kings, since the action of the Reva took place in the sky.
Even Viranchi cannot recount the virtues of the Reva; I tell of Vyasatirtha especially, only as I have heard it.
Where visible proof is seen even in the Kali age: a bird cannot pass over it without being pierced by a most cruel spike.
I shall tell you its origin briefly, prince. Long ago, great king, there was the sage Parashara;
he practised fierce austerity in the water of the Ganga, O Bharata; he entered the water of the Jahnavi and stayed there by breath control.
When the twelfth year was complete he came out of the water and came to a village for alms; there a girl was staying in a boat.
There he saw a lovely girl left by others; seeing her, tormented by desire, he spoke sweet words:
Enjoy me today — who are you, doe-eyed one? — for I am full of desire; seated in the boat on the river bank you agitate my mind.
Thus addressed, she bowed to the best of sages: "I guard the boat, brahmin, but I do not know my master.
This is my age, brahmin; the rest you should know yourself." Thus addressed by her, he meditated a moment and said this:
By the power of knowledge, good lady, I know your origin; you are not a fisherman's daughter but a lovely princess.
The girl said: "Tell me, brahmin, who my father is, from whose womb I was born, in what line I was born, and how I am a fisherman's daughter."
Parashara said: "I shall tell you of your father, as you ask me. There was a king named Vasu in the lunar line, valiant,
lord of Jambudvipa, good lady, and terror of his enemies; he had seven hundred wives and ten sons.
He protected the people with dharma and was always devoted to the worship of Shiva. The mlecchas dwelling in Shakadvipa were hostile to him,
and to subdue them he crossed the great ocean, with his sons and servants, showing great valour.
A battle was begun by them with Vasu, fair one, and all the mlecchas were conquered by Vasu, bearer of the earth;
he made them tributaries together with their servants, forces and vehicles. His chief queen was your doe-eyed mother;
while the king was away she had her period — for women desire is always stronger at that time,
especially in the fertile season, when they are pierced by Love's arrows. Burning with desire, the fair-eyed one thought:
'I shall send a messenger today to King Vasu.' Summoned, a swift messenger was told, 'Go to the king.'
The messenger said: 'King Vasu, destroyer of enemies, has gone to a foreign kingdom, queen; it is impossible to go there without ships, lovely one;
all the vessels have been taken to the other shore.' At his words the woman grew dejected, tormented by passion.
Seeing the queen, a friend said: 'Why do you grieve? Send a letter, queen, in the hand of a parrot somehow;
a bird can cross the ocean, lovely one.' A scribe was summoned there: 'Write a letter at my command:
Without you, King Vasu, the chief queen cannot live; her season has come; consider everything.'
It was written on birch bark by the scribe; a parrot in its cage was brought there near her.
The queen said to it: 'Take the letter, parrot, and go.' Then the bird went quickly to King Vasu,
and the letter was dropped by the parrot, sent by Satyabhama. The lord of men considered the letter's meaning and took his seed;
making an unfailing packet, the renowned one gave it to the parrot in reply: 'Go to the queen.'
Bowing to King Vasu, it took the seed and set off; reaching over the ocean, the parrot went as it pleased.
Thinking the parrot carried flesh, a hawk rushed at it there; the parrot was struck by the hawk with a blow of its beak, O Bharata,
and as it fainted, that seed fell into the water; there the king's seed was swallowed by a fish.
The fish was caught by fishermen and brought to their home; when they cut it open they saw twins,
like the moon's disc and equal in lustre to the sun's radiance; seeing them, all the fishermen on the bank of the Jahnavi were astonished,
and delighted they all went to the headman's house; giving the son to the king, he brought up the daughter.
So you, lady of fair hips, are not a fisherman's daughter." Then she pondered the words of Parashara.
Thus addressed by him, she gave herself to him, lord of men; the virtuous one said, "O brahmin, let the fishy smell be removed."
Then by the power of his yoga that girl was made fragrant with a divine scent; kindling a fire,
and circumambulating the fire, he lifted her up then, and in the midst of the blazing fire he touched the places of love.
Knowing the brahmin eager with desire, she grew afraid, prince, and the girl suddenly said: "It is day, and people are near."
Then, as he meditated for a moment, a darkness came, filling the sky, dear one, by which everything around was covered.
Then in secret with that doe-eyed girl, burning with desire, he enjoyed the pleasure of a woman in wonder.
Then within a muhurta she was burdened with offspring: a boy there, with matted hair, handsome, bearing a staff,
bearing a water-pot, tranquil, a girdle adorning his waist, wearing the sacred thread on his shoulder, free of Vishnu's maya.
The mother was alarmed there seeing her son's quickness; trembling, the girl went to the sage for refuge:

Protect me, protect me, best of sages, great sage Parashara! A most wonderful brahmin has been born, wearing a loincloth and girdle,
skandapuran:109:58	staff in hand, with matted hair, adorned with an upper garment. Parashara said: "Do not fear; a son has been born, and you will become a virgin again.
Your name will be Satyavati, and your second name Gandhayojana; a king named Shantanu will be your husband,
and you will be his first queen, the ornament of the lunar line. Go to your own dwelling, good lady, restored to your former form.
Do not be troubled at this; you have seen the power of my knowledge." Having said this, the brahmin went away, and the girl went to dry land.
She bowed to her son with supreme devotion, prostrating with eight limbs out of love; seeing him about to depart, Satyavati said to her son:
You should grant me my wish, if you have love for your mother; teach me something by which I may attain perfection.
Vyasa said: "Always strive in the worship of the Lord, mother." Then at her son's words she became dejected, delight of Pandu.
Yojanagandha said: "From separation from you, son, I shall die, not otherwise; there is no love like that for a son, no strength like that of a brother."
The son said: "Do not despair, for what my father said is true; in time of distress you should remember me for the accomplishment of your purpose,
and I shall carry you across your troubles; forgive your son, mother." Having said this, Vyasa went away, and the girl went to her father's house.
The son of Parashara settled there in the middle of the forest. At the end of the Treta age and the beginning of the Dvapara, lord of men,
Vyasa was born, as Narada announced to Viranchi, a sage of great power, the son of Parashara,
born of the fisherman's daughter on the bank of the Jahnavi, know this. At Narada's word the best of the gods came —
the Sun, the Grandsire and Shakra, surrounded by hosts of sages; each gave his blessing and said, "Well done, well done."
The Grandsire performed the birth rites and other sacraments for the child: Dvaipayana, being born on an island, Parasharya from Parashara,
Krishna from his dark body; he surpasses even the giver of oblations. He was anointed by Viranchi and the hosts of sages again and again:
You are Vyasa for all the worlds, they said, and departed. Then Krishna Dvaipayana began a pilgrimage to the holy places.
He bathed in the Ganga, at Kedara and Pushkara, at Gaya and the holy place Naimisha, and in the Sarasvati at Kurukshetra;
he went to Mahakala in Ujjayini and then to Somanatha; the great sage Vyasa bathed throughout the earth bounded by the ocean.
Wandering, he reached the Narmada, the river born of Rudra's body; seeing the Narmada with joy, his mind found rest, lord of the earth.
He practised vast austerity resorting to the bank of the Narmada: in summer amid five fires, in the rains lying on bare ground,
in winter in wet clothes, meditating on Maheshvara, maker of creation and dissolution, the indestructible Sadashiva,
daily worshipping the Siddheshvara linga, delight of Pandu. By worship of the Siddhalinga and the power of meditation and yoga,
the Lord became manifest to Krishna Dvaipayana: "I am pleased with you, brahmin; ask a good boon."
Vyasa said: "If you are pleased with me, god, if a boon is to be given me, be manifest yourself on the bank of the Narmada today, lord,
and grant me knowledge of past and future by your grace, Maheshvara." The Lord said: "So be it for you, brahmin, by my grace, no doubt;
captured by your devotion I am manifest on the bank of the Narmada." Having said this, the god went to Kailasa, best of mountains.
He took a wife, and when a son was born to him, it was attended by all the gods headed by Indra and Brahma.
Learning of the son's birth, the best of sages headed by Parashara came, in the course of their pilgrimage:
Manu, Atri, Vishnu, Harita, Yajnavalkya, Ushanas, Angiras, Yama, Apastamba, Samvarta, Katyayana and Brihaspati,
and thousands of others, lakhs and crores in many ways — all the best of the twice-born arrived at Vyasa's lovely holy hermitage.
Seeing the chiefs of brahmins, Vyasa rose eagerly, first bowed to his father and then gave them greeting;
with joined palms he spoke these words: "My joy is lifted up by seeing and speaking with you.
Forest vegetables and forest fruits — these I shall give to all of you, beginning with my father."
He bowed to each of them, all bound by their observances. Then, seeing the brahmin Dvaipayana bowing there,
they blessed him with blessings of victory and then looked at one another; Parashara was looked at by all the bulls among sages:
Give an answer to Krishna Dvaipayana, dear one. Thus addressed by them all, the blessed Parashara
told his son Vyasa what the sages wished: "They do not wish to eat on the southern bank for fear of breaking their vows, son,
though they wish to eat, because of your special faith." Vyasa said: "I will do what is fitting for you; stay here a moment,
while I go to the river and act according to rule." Having said this, he became pure and went to the bank of the Narmada,
and suddenly uttered a hymn; hear it, lord of people.

Vyasa said: "Victory, goddess, salutation, boon-giver, giver of welfare; victory, crusher of sin, trident in hand; victory, you who dissolve into Bhairava's body; victory, goddess to whom the Grandsire bows;

victory, ever saluted by Bhaskara and Shakra; victory, boon-giver, daughter of Shanmukha's father; victory, you who consist of the host of the gods' bodies; victory, daughter of the earth, flowing to the ocean;
victory, victory, you who adorn all the worlds; victory, destroyer of sorrow and poverty; victory, you who increase sons and wives; victory, goddess, lovely to see, remover of sin."
Whoever recites this hymn made by Vyasa in Shiva's presence, or at home with a pure heart, free of desire and anger — Vyasa is pleased with him, and the bull-borne god is pleased.
Praised thus, the goddess Narmada then spoke. Narmada said: "I am pleased by your praise, great sage Vyasa;
whatever boon you rightly desire, I shall give it all to you." Vyasa said: "If you are pleased with me, goddess, if a boon is to be given me,
you should give me hospitality on the northern bank." Narmada said: "What you have thought is improper, Vyasa; you are going astray.
Even Indra, Chandra and Yama cannot make me flow off my course; ask for something else, child, whatever is rare on earth."
Hearing these words of the goddess, Vyasa then fainted; his toil had become vain, and he fell to the ground.
The whole earth shook with its mountains, woods and forests. Knowing Vyasa to have fainted, the gods came to Parashara;
all the gods came, crying out in dismay; lifting Vyasa up, they spoke to the best of rivers:
He has toiled for the sake of brahmins, for the sake of your name, best of rivers; for the sake of cows and brahmins one should give up one's life.
Thus quickly addressed by Brahma and the gods, the Narmada gave way from her banks; bathed all around by the Reva, he was purified by her water,
and, conscious again, this son of Satyavati bowed together with the gods to the Narmada. Vyasa said: "All the holy places of the gods are in you; the fruit is appointed, though my fortune is poor."
Narmada said: "Wherever you lead, great-souled Vyasa, upholder of dharma — whether the path of the mountain named Sumeru, of the Vindhya or of another — I shall go by your path, blessed."
Thus addressed, the mighty Vyasa, son of Satyavati, moved the bulls among sages from the southern side to his own hermitage.
The mighty one, staff in hand, with cries of "Hum!", prince — frightened by Vyasa's cries, the daughter of Rudra moved,
and the goddess was set on her course there as he showed the way with his staff. Seeing the goddess following Vyasa's path, the gods headed by Indra
rained flowers on Vyasa and the kinnaras sang praises; the brahmins headed by Parashara became wide-eyed with joy:
What can we do here? By your greatness and your deed the boon has been won. Vyasa said: "Having practised vast austerity and given gifts of great fruit,
this alone should men do: gratify the good. You fortunate ones, well distinguished, are now worthy of favour;
therefore stay in my holy hermitage, no doubt; the hospitality is of vegetables and leaves mixed with water."
It was accepted by all the brahmins headed by Parashara: "Take shelter in the holy hermitage on the northern bank of the Narmada."
Markandeya said: The best of the twice-born performed their bathing and offerings, and then, going to the Vyasakunda, had the oblation properly performed;
with bilva fruits and bilva leaves, absorbed in meditation, they offered: Gautama, Bhrigu and Mandavya, Narada and Lomasha,
Parashara, Shankha, Kaushika and the sage Chyavana, Pippalada, Vasishtha and Nachiketas of great austerity,
Vishvamitra and Agastya, Uddalaka and Yama, Shandilya, Jaimini, Kavya, Yajnavalkya, Ushanas and Angiras,
Atri, Shatatapa, Bharata and Mudgala, the mighty Vatsyayana, Samvarta and Shakti,
Jatukarna, Bharadvaja and the Valakhilyas and others; single-minded, O king, the brahmins performed mantra and ritual.
Then a linga rose up, shining like the blazing fire of doom; seeing the three-eyed god, Vyasa bowed with eight limbs.
Having again given their blessing to Vyasa, the brahmins then departed. From then on, knower of truth, the holy place has been renowned, son of Pandu.
The rule of bathing and giving, and the time at which it is established, I shall tell you entirely, and your brothers too, son of Pandu.
On the fourteenth of the dark fortnight of Kartika, best of kings, the man who fasts with devotion should keep vigil at night
and bathe the Lord with devotion with honey, milk and ghee,
with curd mixed with sugar or with kusha water, and worship Maheshvara with fragrant sandal;
then worship him with fragrant flowers and bilva leaves, with white lotuses, jasmine, kusha flowers, unbroken rice and the like,
with datura flowers and with gentle and unsurpassed juices; one should worship the unsurpassed Dvipeshvara with supreme devotion,
and worship the supreme Lord with mandara and other flowers. By the gift of a pavilion of jaggery the sin earned in a day,
and by a hundred pavilions of jaggery the sin earned in a month perishes; with a thousand that of six months, with twice that that of twelve years;
sin produced since birth is destroyed by ten thousand. On the full moon, best of kings, one should bathe with devotion,
performing it by the rule stated in the mantras, destroying sin; and the Varuna bath too is to be known as destroying all sins.
One should satisfy the gods, ancestors and men according to rule, O king; bathed, one should recite a single verse of the Rik and gain the fruit of the Sama Veda;
the Yajur Veda and the Atharvan — one gains everything by the Gayatri. One should recite the eight-syllabled mantra, or the solar or Shaiva one,
or the Vaishnava twelve-syllabled mantra. One should honour with devotion brahmins marked with all good signs,
devoted to their own dharma, free of hypocrisy and greed. Those with missing or extra limbs, the fallen, those who serve shudras,
one in whose house is a vrishali and who lives on a shudra's food, the sons of remarried women, the wicked, those given to reviling the guru,
those without Vedic study, sophists, those who live like crows — such one should avoid at shraddha, in giving and in vows.
Better a brahmin who merely recites the Gayatri and is truly learned than one who has mastered the four sciences but eats everything and sells everything;
such one should avoid at shraddha, vows and gifts of gold. Sandals, clothing, a bed, an umbrella or a seat —
whoever gives these to a brahmin with devotion is honoured in heaven. There the actual cow is regarded as equal to the sesame cow.
The givers of the sesame cow, the givers of their own property, the givers of a black antelope skin and the givers of an elephant,
the givers of a maiden and of learning, attain the imperishable world. A pair of draught oxen with a fee, furnished with grain and implements,
one should have given for the fulfilment of all desires — this I say in truth. One should wind a thread around the Lord, or around a tree,
or around the temple with supreme devotion, or the supreme Lord; then circumambulation should be made by men, without a shudra.
Jambu and Plaksha are the continents, and Shalmali, O king, Kusha, Krauncha, Shaka and seventh Pushkara —
the earth bounded by the seven oceans is encircled by him, O Bharata. At Dvipeshvara, king of kings, the release of a bull by those with senses controlled —
by releasing a bull one attains the world of the Lord. The bull that is white on its face, forehead and feet,
and white on its tail and mouth, is a sight of heaven; such a one is called nila; one should give it at auspicious Dvipeshvara.
Even countless lowly people go to heaven, lord of the earth, to the world of the Sun, of Chandeshvara, and to the city of the discus-bearer;
he enjoys the world at will by the power of Vyasatirtha. Then one should honour brahmins with their wives there with devotion,
and give white gems and garments to a brahmin, making two circumambulations: "May the guru of the world be pleased with me."
There is no kinsman equal to a brahmin in this world or the next, who protects one fallen into the most dreadful world of Yama.
Men with supreme devotion, reflecting on the meaning of the Vedas and shastras, who remember the great god Dvipeshvara while staying at home —
for them there arises no grief, no loss and no evil deed. First one should worship there the linga Siddheshvara, O king,
where the fortunate son of Satyavati attained perfection; by worshipping this very one the sage Parasharya became perfected.
Those who give up their lives at that holy place, O king, go to the supreme world; there is no need for deliberation.

One who dies in the water, sunk in it, dwells in heaven a thousand years, by a fall sixteen, in great battle sixty, at a cattle raid eighty, and by fasting to death, O Bharata, the goal is imperishable.
And by that very yoga the imperishable goal is attained; going then to the Sun's world, they go on to Shiva's world.
The father, the grandfather and the great-grandfather, having experienced it, watch for one of their own lineage to come,
one who remains in the lineage and gives sesame water, on the full moons of Kartika, Magha and especially Vaishakha;
they go to heaven at the end by the power of their own sons. All this I have told you, the auspicious fruit of Dvipeshvara.
Whoever recites it on rising at dawn, and the man who hears it, O king, is also freed from sins and rejoices in Shiva's abode.
The Lord of all holy places, made by bulls among sages, grants the desires of all creatures on the Reva, best of kings.
Yudhishthira said: "Tell me briefly how the holy place named Prabhasa of great fruit came to be, and the path of the stairway to heaven."
Markandeya said: The unlucky wife of the Sun, renowned as Prabha, long ago worshipped Shambhu with fierce austerity.
She lived on air for a year, devoted to meditation on Shiva; then Mahadeva was pleased with Prabha, delight of Pandu,
and said: "Why do you torment yourself, young woman? Tell me your purpose. Between me and Bhaskara there is no difference."
Prabha said: "There is no other god, Shambhu; my husband never cherishes me. Whether he is said to have qualities or to be without qualities and possessions,
whether dear or hateful, a husband is a woman's god. I am burned by being unlucky in the midst of the world, Maheshvara;
having found no happiness from my husband, I torment myself for that reason, Maheshvara." The god said: "You will be dear to Bhaskara by my power."
Parvati said: "She will not be dear to Bhaskara by your word alone; the toil would be in vain — what then would become of Prabha?"
At the goddess's words Rudra called to mind the destroyer of darkness; the Sun came from the sky to the northern bank of the Narmada.
The Sun said: "Why have I been summoned, god, destroyer of the asura Andhaka?" The god said: "Cherish Prabha, Sun, with supreme contentment;
dwell always in Prabha's house, destroyer of frost." Having thus obtained a boon from the god, Prabha installed Shankara and said:
Stay here with a portion of yourself and open this holy place, sinless one. Markandeya said: The linga containing all gods was installed, delight of Pandu;
it is named Prabhaseshvara, rare in all the world. The other holy places bear fruit in time;
but Prabhasa, king of kings, gives the fruit of merit at once; on the seventh in the month of Magha it gives special fruit.
Whoever has a horse given there to a brahmin as prescribed, O king, attains the world of Indra or goes to the world of the Sun.
Misfortune is destroyed there by merely bathing, son of Pandu. Whoever at that holy place with devotion gives the gift of a maiden,
should have her given in marriage to a brahmin, delight of Pandu, to a brahmin of equal age, of good family and wealthy;
whoever gives thus, great king, even if laden with great sins, his sin perishes like salt in water.
The sin arising from betraying one's master, the sin arising from theft, the sin of giving false witness, of those who follow the ways of chandalas,
hypocrisy, cutting down trees, the sin arising from going to those one should not go to, that arising from village fraud, poisoning or deception,
what arises from selling learning, sin arising from contact, the dreadful sin of betraying one's wife and that arising from all betrayal, O king,
the sin of killing a brahmin, the sin of one who seizes land, the sin of killing a cow and of offences against the guru, the fire and brahmins —
Jambu and Plaksha are the continents, and Shalmali, O king, Kusha, Krauncha, Shaka and seventh Pushkara —
that sin dissolves by the gift of a maiden, son of Pandu; piercing through the world of the sun, one goes to the auspicious world
and sports dwelling in Rudra's world for as long as fourteen Indras reign; when all sin is destroyed, by his disposition he becomes Shiva.
So long does he wander that holy place Prabhasa, delight of Pandu; he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice — this truth was spoken by the Lord.
The gift of a cow is of great merit, destroying all sins; there, reverently, a real cow, and likewise a water cow,
the giver of a sesame cow and the giver of a horse, the giver of a maiden and of learning attain the imperishable world.
With abundant cloth, full of milk, furnished with grain and implements — one desiring all things should have such a cow given, best of kings.
The earth bounded by the seven oceans is encircled by him, O Bharata. At Dvipeshvara, king of kings, the release of a bull by those with senses controlled
should be done at all times, and especially on the fourteenth.
You who cut off worldly existence, named Arta, destroyer of affliction, goddess standing at the door of heaven, have compassion on me.
The Ganga said: "Practise vast austerity toward Shankara, naga." Then he practised austerity, the supreme worship of the Lord,
and as he meditated on the god he became endowed with self-control; when a hundred years were complete, the guru of the world, besought,
came and stood near him and spoke gentle words: "Choose an excellent boon, mighty serpent."
The serpent said: "If you are pleased with me, god, trident-bearer, to grant a boon, then give me a place of my own, bull-borne one."
The Lord said: "I am pleased, mighty-armed one; go quickly to the lovely Reva and bathe according to rule on its holy southern bank."
Having said this, the god vanished, and Vasuki in haste, in the form of a python, entered the water of the Narmada.
By his path there arose an excellent stream of the Jahnavi; the serpent was cleansed of his impurity in the water of the Narmada,
and the Lord was installed there on the Narmada, Yudhishthira; hence Nageshvara on earth destroys all sins.
On the eighth and fourteenth one should bathe Shiva with honey; freed from all sins, one becomes like fire.
Men without sons who bathe at the confluence, son of Pritha, obtain fine sons, even like Kartavirya.
Those devoted to fasting who perform shraddha there with devotion rescue their own from hell, prince.
Thus I have told you, especially out of affection. Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the excellent Markandeshvara,
on the southern bank of the Narmada, auspicious, saluted by the gods; this holy place, more secret than the secret, I have told to no one.
It was installed by me, holy, granting the enjoyment of heaven and liberation; knowledge arose in me right there by the grace of Shankara.
Whoever meditates on another hymn and recites the "drupadad" in the water is also freed from a dreadful flood of sin, delight of Pandu,
whether of speech, of mind or born of deeds, son of Pandu; restraining the five senses and facing the south,
whoever recites it in the water with devotion — so said Shankara. Whoever performs shraddha there with devotion, prince,
his ancestors are satisfied until the deluge. With amalaka fruits, jujubes, bilva, unbroken rice or water,
whoever makes offerings there to the departed — the departed go to a good goal.
Sankarshana is famous on earth as destroying sin; austerity was practised long ago, O king, on the lovely bank of the Narmada
by Balabhadra, king of kings, beneficial to living beings; and there too, in the presence of the gods, prince,
Shambhu with Uma and Keshava dwell. Whoever there, with devotion, having conquered anger and the senses,
bathes Shiva with a mantra on the eleventh of the bright fortnight, and whoever with devotion has shraddha given there for the departed,
goes to the supreme place, as Balabhadra declared. Then, king of kings, one should go to the excellent Manmatheshvara.
A man who merely bathes there, O king, does not see Yama's world; a childless woman who bathes the god, delight of Pandu,
obtains a son, son of Pritha, truthful and firm in his vows. A man who bathes there, O king, a sage with restrained mind,
and fasts with supreme devotion, gains the fruit of a thousand cows. Men of devoted mind who dance there,
and keep an auspicious vigil at night with song and music — Mahadeva Manmatheshvara with Ambika is pleased with them.
What can Yama do in his wrath? He does not even see him. It was installed there by Kama, and for this reason, O king,
by the gift of food there, O king, the excellent fruit is declared; Manmatheshvara on earth is a stairway on the path to heaven.
